topics.title: Traveling Waves
topics.summary: A disturbance that keeps its shape as it moves: amplitude sets its size, k and ω set its wavelength and period, and their ratio sets its speed.
topics.equation: y(x,t) = A cos(kx − ωt)  ·  v = ω/k = fλ = √(T/μ)

topics.title: Standing Waves & Normal Modes
topics.summary: Fix both ends and only a discrete set of patterns survives, each oscillating in place at its own frequency.

topics.title: Superposition & Interference
topics.summary: In a linear medium, waves simply add: crest on crest reinforces, crest on trough cancels, and two close frequencies beat.

topics.title: Fourier Series
topics.summary: Any reasonable periodic shape is a sum of sines and cosines at whole-number multiples of one fundamental frequency.
topics.equation: f(x) = a_{0}/2 + Σ [a_{n} cos(nπx/L) + b_{n} sin(nπx/L)]

topics.title: Sound Waves
topics.summary: Longitudinal waves in air: pressure and displacement are 90° out of phase, and a moving source or listener shifts the frequency you hear (Doppler).

topics.title: General Solution f(x − vt) + g(x + vt)
topics.summary: d'Alembert: every solution of the 1D wave equation is a right-mover plus a left-mover, both fixed by the initial shape and velocity.

topics.title: Boundary Conditions
topics.summary: What the end of the string is allowed to do decides how waves reflect: a fixed end flips the pulse, a free end doesn't.

topics.title: Phase & Superposition
topics.summary: The phase constant φ slides a wave in time; sine and cosine are the same wave a quarter period apart, and adding same-frequency waves only changes amplitude and phase.
topics.equation: a cos ωt + b sin ωt = R cos(ωt − δ)  ·  R = √(a^{2} + b^{2})  ·  tan δ = b/a

topics.title: Original Sims
topics.summary: My own simulations, each built to check one piece of the math against first principles rather than just show it.

tools.name: PhET: Wave on a String
tools.my_note: Best for physical intuition. Set Oscillate mode + No End to see pure traveling waves. Switch end to Fixed for standing waves. The three end modes (fixed/loose/no end) are the cleanest way to see how boundary conditions change everything. Turn on Rulers + Stopwatch to measure λ and T and check v = λ/T, then raise Tension at a fixed Frequency and watch λ stretch (v = √(T/μ)).
tools.controls: Wave mode: Manual / Oscillate / Pulse · String end: Fixed / Loose / No End · Amplitude, Frequency, Pulse Width, Damping, Tension · Rulers, Stopwatch, Reference Line · Restart String

tools.name: PhET: Fourier: Making Waves
tools.my_note: On the Discrete screen, pick the square waveform and raise Harmonics from 1 to 11 while watching the Sum graph: the corners sharpen, but the overshoot beside each jump never shrinks in height (Gibbs). Compare it with Infinite Harmonics. With a single harmonic, flip Series between sin and cos: it's the same wave shifted a quarter period, which is §8 in one click. Finish on the Wave Game screen. Matching a mystery wave by setting amplitudes is the best self-test for reading a spectrum.
tools.controls: Screens: Discrete / Wave Game / Wave Packet · Waveform presets (sinusoid, triangle, square, sawtooth, wave packet, custom) · Harmonics count with one amplitude slider per harmonic · Series: sin / cos · Function of: space / time / space & time · Equation forms · Infinite Harmonics · Sound

tools.name: PhET: Sound Waves
tools.my_note: Start on Intro with Listener Audio on and change only Frequency, then only Amplitude, so you hear pitch vs. loudness before reaching for equations. On Measure, switch Sound Mode to Pulse, fire a single pulse and time it over a known distance to get the speed of sound yourself. Two Sources and Reflection show interference in air, and Air Pressure lets you pump the air out of the box and watch the sound die. There's no Doppler here; use Falstad Ripple Tank or oPhysics for that.
tools.controls: Screens: Intro / Measure / Two Sources / Reflection / Air Pressure · Frequency, Amplitude · Sound Mode: Continuous / Pulse (Fire Pulse) · Listener Audio · Wall Position and Wall Angle (Reflection) · Air Density in Box (Air Pressure) · Clear Waves
tools.todo: Confirm which measuring tools (ruler, stopwatch) the Measure screen offers.

tools.name: PhET: Normal Modes
tools.my_note: In One Dimension, set Number of Masses to 3, press Zero Positions, then raise exactly one slider in the Normal Mode Spectrum. Every mass now moves at that one frequency, which is what a normal mode is. Excite two modes at once and the motion stops looking periodic, even though it's just two clean oscillations added together. Then go to 10 masses and look at the higher modes: each shape is sin(nπx/L) sampled at the masses, which is where a continuous string's harmonics come from.
tools.controls: Screens: One Dimension / Two Dimensions · Number of Masses · Normal Mode Spectrum: amplitude and phase per mode · Show Phases · Show Springs · Initial Positions / Zero Positions

tools.name: Falstad: Fourier Series
tools.my_note: Click Square, then drag Number of Terms slowly to the right. The red partial sum converges everywhere except right beside the jump, where a ~9% overshoot only gets narrower: that's the Gibbs phenomenon, and it never goes away at finite N. Hover over a bar to see that single harmonic drawn in yellow, and right-click a bar to cut the series off there. Tick Mag/Phase View and press Phase Shift: the magnitudes stay put and only the phases move (§8). Turn on Sound to hear the harmonics pile up.
tools.controls: Waveforms: Sine, Cosine, Triangle, Sawtooth, Square, Noise · Phase Shift · Clear (then draw your own) · Clip, Resample, Quantize, Rectify, Full Rectify, High-Pass Filter · Number of Terms · Mag/Phase View, Log View · Sound, Playing Frequency

tools.name: Falstad: Loaded String
tools.my_note: Press Center Pluck and read the mode-amplitude graph under the string: only odd modes light up, because every even mode has a node exactly where you plucked. Set Display to Left+Right to watch the standing wave split into two traveling waves (§6). With only a handful of loads, the higher modes oscillate below n·f₁ and travel more slowly. That's dispersion, the discrete string failing to act like a continuous one.
tools.controls: Fundamental, Center Pluck, Clear · Stopped, Driving Force, Sound, Log View · Mouse: Pluck string / Shape string · Display: Phases, Phase Cosines, Phasors, Modes, Left+Right · Simulation Speed, Damping, Force Frequency, Number of Loads, Tension · Resonance Freq

tools.name: Falstad: Ripple Tank
tools.my_note: Choose Example → Two Sources and find the nodal lines, the calm rays between bright fringes. Raise Source Frequency and they crowd together, because the fringe angle depends on λ/d. For §5, pick Doppler Effect 1: wavefronts bunch up ahead of the moving source and stretch out behind it, and Sonic Boom shows the Mach cone once the source outruns its own waves. Tick Stopped to freeze a frame and count wavelengths, or 3-D View to see the field as a surface.
tools.controls: Example menu (Single Source, Two Sources, Single/Double Slit, Doppler Effect 1 & 2, Sonic Boom, …) · Source Frequency, Simulation Speed, Resolution · Stopped, 3-D View, Fixed Edges · draw waves and walls with the mouse; right-click to add objects

tools.name: oPhysics: Superposition of Transverse Waves
tools.my_note: The red and blue waves travel in opposite directions and the magenta curve is their sum. Give them equal amplitude and wavelength first: the sum stops traveling and just oscillates in place, a standing wave built from two traveling ones. Then detune one wavelength slightly and use Step Animation to see why the pattern no longer stands still.
tools.controls: Sliders: wave speed, amplitude and wavelength of each wave · Step Animation · play / pause

tools.name: oPhysics: Wave Pulse Superposition
tools.my_note: Set one pulse's height negative and equal in size to the other. At the moment they overlap the string is flat, yet both pulses come out unchanged: the energy was hiding in the string's velocity. Then give the pulses different widths. They still pass straight through each other, which is the linearity behind y = f(x − vt) + g(x + vt).
tools.controls: Sliders: height and width of each pulse, animation speed · Start / Stop
tools.todo: Check that the height sliders go negative (inverted pulses).

tools.name: oPhysics: Standing Waves
tools.my_note: Start with the string, step through the harmonics and count nodes: harmonic n has n + 1 of them, ends included. Then switch to an air column and show the pressure variation wave alongside the displacement wave. Displacement nodes sit exactly where the pressure swings hardest, which ties standing waves straight back to sound (§5).
tools.controls: Buttons: string or air column, harmonic number · Checkboxes: transverse displacement, longitudinal displacement, pressure variation

tools.name: oPhysics: Wave Pulse Reflection (Free/Fixed)
tools.my_note: Send the pulse into a fixed end with the undisturbed incident and reflected waves showing. The reflected 'ghost' is inverted and the real string is the sum, so the endpoint never moves. Switch to a free end and the ghost comes back upright, so at the end the two add and the endpoint swings to twice the pulse height. That's the whole difference between y = 0 and ∂y/∂x = 0 at the boundary.
tools.controls: Checkboxes: fixed end / free end · show undisturbed incident wave · show undisturbed reflected wave

tools.name: oPhysics: Beats
tools.my_note: Enter two close frequencies (440 and 442 Hz), press play, and count the swells in loudness: you should hear |f₁ − f₂| = 2 per second. Press play again after every change. The page sends one tone to each ear, so on headphones the beat is made by your brain (binaural beats); play it through speakers so the two waves genuinely add in the air. Widen the gap to 10 and then 30 Hz and notice where beating turns into roughness.
tools.controls: Left-ear and right-ear frequency inputs (Hz) · Play / Stop

tools.name: oPhysics: Oscillations and Phase Shift
tools.my_note: Set the phase shift to 90° and watch the two points on the reference circle: one is a quarter turn ahead, and its graph is a cosine where the other is a sine. Then try 180° (perfectly opposite motion) and 360° (identical again). φ is nothing more than the angle between two points going around the same circle.
tools.controls: Phase shift between the two oscillators · play / pause
tools.todo: Check the actual slider names (phase shift, frequency?).

tools.name: oPhysics: Doppler & Sonic Boom
tools.my_note: Keep the observer still and set the source to half the wave speed: the fronts ahead are squeezed to half their normal spacing and stretched out behind. Push the source past the wave speed to see the fronts pile into a Mach cone. Then hold the source still and move the observer instead. The spacing stays even, yet the observer still meets fronts more often: a different mechanism with a different formula.
tools.controls: Sliders: source speed, observer speed
tools.todo: Confirm the slider names and whether the page shows the observed frequency.

tools.name: Walter Fendt: Standing Wave via Reflection
tools.my_note: Press Start with only the incident wave (red) showing, then add the reflected wave (blue), then the resultant (black): you watch a standing wave get assembled from two traveling ones. Switch between reflection from a fixed end and from a free end and watch the endpoint. A fixed end is always a node (N), a free end always an antinode (A). Use Single steps at T/8 to catch the instant the red and blue waves cancel everywhere.
tools.controls: Reflection from a fixed end / free end · Reset, Start / Pause / Resume · Slow motion (10×) · Animation or Single steps (T/4, T/8, T/12, T/24) · show incident, reflected, resultant wave

tools.name: The Physics Aviary: Standing Waves Lab
tools.embed_note: Link only: the site is behind a Cloudflare bot check, which shows up as a blank frame when embedded.
tools.my_note: Click Begin, then turn on Ghosting and Slow Motion so the standing wave traces out its envelope. Overlay the three Show Fundamental options (Node/Node, Node/Antinode, Antinode/Antinode) and Activate Grid to work out which end conditions and lengths could produce the pattern on screen. That node/antinode bookkeeping is §7's boundary logic applied to §2.
tools.controls: Begin · Enable Slow Motion · Enable Ghosting · Show Fundamental: Node/Node, Node/Antinode, Antinode/Antinode · Show Full Wave · Show 2nd Harmonic · Activate Grid

tools.name: Andrew Duffy (BU): Standing Wave
tools.my_note: Pick n = 1, press Play, and watch the traces: one wave traveling right, one traveling left, and their sum, which stays put. Step >> through frame by frame and check that the nodes of the sum never move while each component slides right through them. Then try n = 2 to 6 and count nodes and antinodes against λ = 2L/n.
tools.controls: Play, Pause, << Step, Step >>, Reset · Harmonic: n = 1 to 6

tools.name: MIT Mathlets: Wave Equation
tools.source: MIT Mathlets (H. Miller, J. Orloff, J.-M. Claus)
tools.my_note: Turn on Solution with Left wave and Right wave. The plucked triangle splits into two half-height copies moving in opposite directions (d'Alembert), and their inverted reflections off the fixed ends are what make the mid-cycle shapes look so odd. Now switch those off, turn on Fourier sum and raise the number of harmonics: the same motion is rebuilt from standing modes, and the corners sharpen only slowly. Click the graph to move the pluck point; plucking at x = 1/3 kills every third harmonic.
tools.controls: Toggles: Solution, Harmonics, Fourier sum, Left wave, Right wave · number-of-harmonics slider · time slider, play (>>) / pause (||), Animation speed · click the graph to move the pluck point

tools.name: MIT Mathlets: Fourier Coefficients
tools.my_note: Pick a target (A–G) and, before touching a slider, predict from its symmetry which terms must vanish; the Sine/Cosine and Odd/Even keys let you test the guess. Then turn on Distance and tune one coefficient at a time to minimize it. Because sines and cosines are orthogonal, each slider's best value doesn't depend on the others, and it lands on the actual Fourier coefficient. Formula shows the integral each slider is secretly approximating.
tools.controls: Targets A–G · Sine / Cosine · All / Odd / Even terms · coefficient sliders with < > fine-tuning · Distance (RMS) · Formula · Reset

tools.name: Dan Russell: Longitudinal Wave Pressure/Displacement
tools.source: Daniel A. Russell, Penn State Acoustics
tools.embed_note: Link only: an animation gallery that reads best as a full page.
tools.my_note: Read this one for the phase bookkeeping. In a right-moving sound wave, pressure and particle velocity are in phase and displacement lags them by 90°; in a left-moving wave the velocity flips sign relative to pressure. Watch the animations with a single particle in mind, then open Show/Hide Math to see it all fall out of Euler's equation, ρ ∂u/∂t = −∂p/∂x.
tools.controls: Animated plots of displacement, particle velocity and pressure for forward and backward waves · Show/Hide Math Equations and Explanation
tools.todo: Check whether the animations can be paused or stepped.

tools.name: Manchester: Sound Wave Pressure vs Displacement
tools.my_note: Follow the red particle: pressure peaks as it passes through its rest position (zero displacement), not when it's pushed furthest. Turn Amplitude to maximum and Speed to minimum, pause at a few points in the cycle, then tick Show displacement wave to confirm it runs a quarter cycle (90°) behind the pressure wave. Pair it with Dan Russell's page for the math behind why.
tools.controls: Play / Pause · Speed · Frequency · Amplitude · Show displacement wave

tools.name: Phase Explorer
tools.my_note: Drag φ and watch A cos(kx − ωt + φ) slide along x, with a rotating phasor beside it so the angle is always visible. Overlay sin and cos to see they're the same wave 90° apart, then add a second wave of the same frequency and read the result's amplitude and phase straight off the phasor sum.
tools.verifies: A_{1} cos ωt + A_{2} cos(ωt + φ) = A cos(ωt + δ) with A^{2} = A_{1}^{2} + A_{2}^{2} + 2A_{1}A_{2} cos φ, checked as phasor sum vs. sampled waveform
tools.controls: Planned: A, k, ω, φ sliders · second wave · phasor diagram · sin/cos overlay

tools.name: d'Alembert
tools.my_note: Draw any initial shape (and optionally an initial velocity) and watch it split into f(x − vt) and g(x + vt), with both halves drawn so the sum is never a black box. Fixed and free ends come later, as mirror-image 'ghost' waves arriving from outside the string.
tools.verifies: y(x,t) = ½[y_{0}(x − vt) + y_{0}(x + vt)] + (1/2v)∫u_{0} ds matches a finite-difference solution of the same initial-value problem
tools.controls: Planned: draw the initial shape and velocity · wave speed v · time scrubber · show f, g, and their sum

tools.name: String FDTD
tools.my_note: A finite-difference time-domain solver for the 1D wave equation with fixed, free, or absorbing ends: the numerical ground truth the other sims get checked against. It shows the Courant number live, so you can watch the scheme blow up the moment vΔt/Δx > 1.
tools.verifies: Energy ½∫(μ y_{t}^{2} + T y_{x}^{2}) dx stays constant without damping, pulses travel at √(T/μ), and the scheme goes unstable exactly when vΔt/Δx > 1
tools.controls: Planned: tension, μ, damping · boundary per end (fixed / free / absorbing) · Δx, Δt with live Courant number · pluck, pulse, or drive

tools.name: Fourier Synth
tools.my_note: Build a waveform from N harmonics, each with its own amplitude and phase, or draw a shape and let the sim compute the coefficients numerically. Listen to it, and watch the Gibbs overshoot settle at about 9% of the jump no matter how large N gets.
tools.verifies: Numerically integrated coefficients match the closed forms (square wave: b_{n} = 4/nπ for odd n), and the energy in the partial sums climbs to the function's energy (Parseval)
tools.controls: Planned: N harmonics · amplitude and phase per harmonic · presets + freehand drawing · audio

tools.name: Mode Decomposition
tools.my_note: Take any string shape, project it onto the normal modes sin(nπx/L), and evolve each mode at its own frequency. The mode sum is drawn on top of the String FDTD solution, so you see the two descriptions agree, or exactly where they don't.
tools.verifies: Σ b_{n} sin(nπx/L) cos(ω_{n}t) agrees with String FDTD to within discretization error, and each mode's energy stays constant on its own
tools.controls: Planned: initial shape (pluck / draw) · number of modes · per-mode energy bars · overlay vs. String FDTD

tools.name: General Solution Explorer
tools.my_note: Nothing on the list lets you pick your own f and g. Choose or type any two functions, form y = f(x − vt) + g(x + vt), and watch the wave-equation residual stay at zero; then try a function that isn't of that form and watch it fail.
tools.verifies: The residual ∂^{2}y/∂t^{2} − v^{2}∂^{2}y/∂x^{2} ≈ 0 for any smooth f and g, and is clearly nonzero for impostors like y = t·sin x
tools.controls: Planned: f and g presets or typed expressions · v · residual map

tools.name: Pressure ↔ Displacement
tools.my_note: The existing tools show this relationship but don't let you probe it. Particles, displacement s(x, t), and pressure p = −B ∂s/∂x sit in three synchronized rows, with a probe you drag to read all three at one point.
tools.verifies: p = −B ∂s/∂x computed from the particle positions equals B k s_{0} sin(kx − ωt), so pressure leads displacement by 90° for a right-moving wave
tools.controls: Planned: amplitude, frequency, bulk modulus B · particle, displacement, and pressure rows · draggable probe
